entries.30077dada977236746c90dfb58f12c404d09c120: <div sID="gen877" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Gen.25" sID="Gen.25"/> <div eID="gen877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen878" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen879" type="x-p"/> The sacred historian, in this chapter, I. Takes his leave of Abraham, with an account, 1. Of his children by another wife, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.1-Gen.25.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. 2. Of his last will and testament, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.5-Gen.25.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. 3. Of his age, death, and burial, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.7-Gen.25.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. II. He takes his leave of Ishmael, with a short account, 1. Of his children, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.12-Gen.25.16">ver. 12-16</reference>. 2. Of his age and death, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.17-Gen.25.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>. III. He enters upon the history of Isaac. 1. His prosperity, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.11">ver. 11</reference>. 2. The conception and birth of his two sons, with the oracle of God concerning them, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.19-Gen.25.26">ver. 19-26</reference>. 3. Their different characters, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.27-Gen.25.28">ver. 27, 28</reference>. 4. Esau's selling his birthright to Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.29-Gen.25.34">ver. 29-34</reference>.
entries.75ce4b801d4229fa46b3cefd19a9eb3b7a188fe3: <div eID="gen879" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen878" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Abraham's Death. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1822.)</title> <div sID="gen880" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Keturah. <hi type="super">2</hi> And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Jokshan begat Sheba, and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the children of Keturah. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac. <hi type="super">6</hi> But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country. <hi type="super">7</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the days of the years of Abraham's life which he lived, an hundred threescore and fifteen years. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full <hi type="italic">of years</hi>; and was gathered to his people. <hi type="super">9</hi> And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Mamre; <hi type="super">10</hi> The field which Abraham purchased of the sons of Heth: there was Abraham buried, and Sarah his wife. <div eID="gen880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen881" type="x-p"/> Abraham lived, after the marriage of Isaac, thirty-five years, and all that is recorded concerning him during the time lies here in a very few verses. We hear no more of God's extraordinary appearances to him or trials of him; for all the days, even of the best and greatest saints, are not eminent days, some slide on silently, and neither come nor go with observation; such were these last days of Abraham. We have here, <div eID="gen881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen882" type="x-p"/> I. An account of his children by Keturah, another wife whom he married after the death of Sarah. He had buried Sarah and married Isaac, the two dear companions of his life, and was now solitary. He wanted a nurse, his family wanted a governess, and it was not good for him to be thus alone. He therefore marries Keturah, probably the chief of his maid-servants, born in his house or bought with money. Marriage is not forbidden to old age. By her he had six sons, in whom the promise made to Abraham concerning the great increase of his posterity was in part fulfilled, which, it is likely, he had an eye to this marriage. The strength he received by the promise still remained in him, to show how much the virtue of the promise exceeds the power of nature. <div eID="gen882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen883" type="x-p"/> II. The disposition which Abraham made of his estate, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.5-Gen.25.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. After the birth of these sons, he set his house in order, with prudence and justice. 1. He made Isaac his heir, as he was bound to do, in justice to Sarah his first and principal wife, and to Rebekah who married Isaac upon the assurance of it, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.36">ch. xxiv. 36</reference>. In this <hi type="italic">all,</hi> which he settled upon Isaac, are perhaps included the promise of the land of Canaan, and the entail of the covenant. Or, God having already made him the heir of the promise, Abraham therefore made him heir of his estate. Our affection and gifts should attend God's. 2. He gave portions to the rest of his children, both to Ishmael, though at first he was sent empty away, and to his sons by Keturah. It was justice to provide for them; parents that do not imitate him in this are worse than infidels. It was prudence to settle them in places distant from Isaac, that they might not pretend to divide the inheritance with him, nor be in any way a care or expense to him. Observe, He did this <hi type="italic">while he yet lived,</hi> lest it should not be done, or not so well done, afterwards. Note, In many cases it is wisdom for men to make their own hands their executors, and what they find to do to do it while they live, as far as they can. These <hi type="italic">sons of the concubines</hi> were sent into the country that lay east from Canaan, and their posterity were called <hi type="italic">the children of the east,</hi> famous for their numbers, <reference osisRef="Judg.6.5">Judg. vi. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.6.33">33</reference>. Their great increase was the fruit of the promise made to Abraham, that God would multiply his seed. God, in dispensing his blessings, does as Abraham did; common blessings he gives to the children of this world, as to the sons of the bond-woman, but covenant-blessings he reserves for the heirs of promise. All that he has is theirs, for they are his Isaacs, from whom the rest shall be for ever separated. <div eID="gen883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen884" type="x-p"/> III. The age and death of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.7-Gen.25.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. He lived 175 years, just 100 years after he came to Canaan; so long he was a sojourner in a strange country. Though he lived long and lived well, though he did good and could ill be spared, yet he died at last. Observe how his death is here described. 1. He <hi type="italic">gave up the ghost.</hi> His life was not extorted from him, but he cheerfully resigned it; into the hands of the Father of spirits he committed his spirit. 2. He <hi type="italic">died in a good old age, an old man;</hi> so God had promised him. His death was his discharge from the burdens of his age: an old man would not <hi type="italic">so</hi> live always. It was also the crown of the glory of his old age. 3. He was <hi type="italic">full of years,</hi> or full of <hi type="italic">life</hi> (as it might be supplied), including all the conveniences and comforts of life. He did not live till the world was weary of him, but till he was weary of the world; he had had enough of it, and desired no more. <hi type="italic">Vixi quantum satis est—I have lived long enough.</hi> A good man, though he should not die old, dies full of days, satisfied with living here, and longing to live in a better place. 4. He <hi type="italic">was gathered to his people.</hi> His body was gathered to the congregation of the dead, and his soul to the congregation of the blessed. Note, Death gathers us to our people. Those that are our people while we live, whether the people of God or the children of this world, are the people to whom death will gather us. <div eID="gen884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen885" type="x-p"/> IV. His burial, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.9-Gen.25.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Here is nothing recorded of the pomp or ceremony of his funeral; only we are told, 1. Who buried him: <hi type="italic">His sons Isaac and Ishmael.</hi> It was the last office of respect they had to pay to their good father. Some distance there had formerly been between Isaac and Ishmael; but it seems either that Abraham had himself brought them together while he lived, or at least that his death reconciled them. 2. Where they buried him: in his own burying-place, which he had purchased, and in which he had buried Sarah. Note, Those that in life have been very dear to each other may not only innocently, but laudably, desire to be buried together, that in their deaths they may not be divided, and in token of their hopes of rising together.
entries.d15683a557f8ba7a8b9bc49a6349ea3ccb650538: <div eID="gen885" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogy of Ishmael. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1822.)</title> <div sID="gen886" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And it came to pass after the death of Abraham, that God blessed his son Isaac; and Isaac dwelt by the well Lahai-roi. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's handmaid, bare unto Abraham: <hi type="super">13</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam, <hi type="super">14</hi> And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa, <hi type="super">15</hi> Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah: <hi type="super">16</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Ishmael, and these <hi type="italic">are</hi> their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations. <hi type="super">17</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the years of the life of Ishmael, an hundred and thirty and seven years: and he gave up the ghost and died; and was gathered unto his people. <hi type="super">18</hi> And they dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he died in the presence of all his brethren. <div eID="gen886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen887" type="x-p"/> Immediately after the account of Abraham's death, Moses begins the story of Isaac (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.11">v. 11</reference>), and tells us where he dwelt and how remarkably God blessed him. Note, The blessing of Abraham did not die with him, but survived to all the children of the promise. But he presently digresses from the story of Isaac, to give a short account of Ishmael, forasmuch as he also was a son of Abraham, and God had made some promises concerning him, which it was requisite we should know the accomplishment of. Observe here what is said, 1. Concerning his children. He had twelve sons, <hi type="italic">twelve princes</hi> they are called (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.16">v. 16</reference>), heads of families, which in process of time became nations, distinct tribes, numerous and very considerable. They peopled a very large continent, that lay between Egypt and Assyria, called <hi type="italic">Arabia.</hi> The names of his twelve sons are recorded. Midian and Kedar we often read of in scripture. And some very good expositors have taken notice of the signification of those three names which are put together (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.14">v. 14</reference>), as containing good advice to us all, <hi type="italic">Mishma, Dumah,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Massa,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">hear, keep silence,</hi> and <hi type="italic">bear;</hi> we have them together in the same order, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.19">Jam. i:19</reference>, <hi type="italic">Be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.</hi> The posterity of Ishmael had not only tents in the fields, wherein they grew rich in times of peace; but they had towns and castles (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.16">v. 16</reference>), wherein they fortified themselves in time of war. Now the number and strength of this family were the fruit of the promise made to Hagar concerning Ishmael (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.10">ch. xvi. 10</reference>), and to Abraham, <reference osisRef="Ge.17.20">ch. xvii. 20</reference> and <reference osisRef="21.13">xxi. 13</reference>. Note, Many that are strangers to the covenants of promise are yet blessed with outward prosperity for the sake of their godly ancestors. <hi type="italic">Wealth and riches shall be in their house.</hi> 2. Concerning himself. Here is an account of his age: He <hi type="italic">lived</hi> 137 <hi type="italic">years</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.17">v. 17</reference>) which is recorded to show the efficacy of Abraham's prayer for him (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.18">ch. xvii. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">O that Ishmael might live before thee!</hi> Here is also an account of his death; he too <hi type="italic">was gathered to his people;</hi> but it is not said that he was <hi type="italic">full of days,</hi> though he lived to so great an age: he was not so weary of the world, nor so willing to leave it, as his good father was. Those words, <hi type="italic">he fell in the presence of all his brethren,</hi> whether they mean, as we take them, <hi type="italic">he died,</hi> or, as others, <hi type="italic">his lot fell,</hi> are designed to show the fulfilling of that word to Hagar (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">ch. xvi. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">He shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren,</hi> that is, he shall flourish and be eminent among them, and shall hold his own to the last. Or he died with his friends about him, which is comfortable.
entries.91a87b5be4f53a12fe42e3cf1a5c12725ec044c6: <div eID="gen887" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Birth of Esau and Jacob. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1837.)</title> <div sID="gen888" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son: Abraham begat Isaac: <hi type="super">20</hi> And Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah to wife, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Padan-aram, the sister to Laban the Syrian. 21 And Isaac intreated the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for his wife, because she <hi type="italic">was</hi> barren: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the children struggled together within her; and she said, If <hi type="italic">it be</hi> so, why <hi type="italic">am</hi> I thus? And she went to enquire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">23</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto her, Two nations <hi type="italic">are</hi> in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and <hi type="italic">the one</hi> people shall be stronger than <hi type="italic">the other</hi> people; and the elder shall serve the younger. <hi type="super">24</hi> And when her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, <hi type="italic">there were</hi> twins in her womb. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the first came out red, all over like a hairy garment; and they called his name Esau. 26 And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob: and Isaac <hi type="italic">was</hi> threescore years old when she bare them. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob <hi type="italic">was</hi> a plain man, dwelling in tents. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of <hi type="italic">his</hi> venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob. <div eID="gen888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen889" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the birth of Jacob and Esau, the twin sons of Isaac and Rebekah: their entrance into the world was (which is not usual) one of the most considerable parts of their story; nor is much related concerning Isaac but what had reference to his father while he lived and to his sons afterwards. For Isaac seems not to have been a man of action, nor much tried, but to have spent his days in quietness and silence. Now concerning Jacob and Esau we are here told, <div eID="gen889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen890" type="x-p"/> I. That they were prayed for. Their parents, after they had been long childless, obtained them by prayer, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.20-Gen.25.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Isaac was forty years old when he was married;</hi> though he was an only son, and the person from whom the promised seed was to come, yet he made no haste to marry. He was sixty years old when his sons were born (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.26">v. 26</reference>), so that, after he was married, he had no child for twenty years. Note, Though the accomplishment of God's promise is always sure, yet it is often slow, and seems to be crossed and contradicted by Providence, that the faith of believers may be tried, their patience exercised, and mercies long waited for may be the more welcome when they come. While this mercy was delayed, Isaac did not approach to a handmaid's bed, as Abraham had done, and Jacob afterwards; for he loved Rebekah, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.67">ch. xxiv. 67</reference>. But, 1. He prayed: he entreated the Lord for his wife. Though God had promised to multiply his family, he prayed for its increase; for God's promises must not supersede, but encourage, our prayers, and be improved as the ground of our faith. Though he had prayed for this mercy very often, and had continued his supplication many years, and it was not granted, yet he did not leave off praying for it; for men ought always to pray, and not to faint (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.1">Luke xviii. 1</reference>), to pray without ceasing, and knock till the door be opened, He prayed <hi type="italic">for</hi> his wife; some read it <hi type="italic">with</hi> his wife. Note, Husbands and wives should pray together, which is intimated in the apostle's caution, that their <hi type="italic">prayers be not hindered,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1 Pet. iii. 7</reference>. The Jews have a tradition that Isaac, at length, took his wife with him to mount Moriah, where God had promised that he would multiply Abraham's seed (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">ch. xxii. 17</reference>), and there, in his prayer with her and for her, pleaded the promise made in that very place. 2. God heard his prayer, and was entreated of him. Note, Children are the gift of God. Those that continue instant in prayer, as Isaac did, shall find, at last, that they did not <hi type="italic">seek in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Isa. xlv. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen891" type="x-p"/> II. That they were prophesied of before they were born, and great mysteries were wrapped up in the prophecies which went before of them, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.22-Gen.25.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. Long had Isaac prayed for a son; and now his wife is with child of two, to recompense him for his long waiting. Thus God often outdoes our prayers, and gives more than we are able to ask or think. Now Rebekah being with child of these two sons, observe here, <div eID="gen891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen892" type="x-p"/> 1. How she was perplexed in her mind concerning her present case: <hi type="italic">The children struggled together within her.</hi> The commotion she felt was altogether extraordinary and made her very uneasy. Whether she was apprehensive that the birth would be her death, or whether she was weary of the intestine tumult, or whether she suspected it to be an ill omen, it seems she was ready to wish that either she had not been with child or that she might die immediately, and not bring forth such a struggling brood: <hi type="italic">If it be so,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">since it is so, Why am I thus?</hi> Before, the want of children was her trouble, now, the struggle of the children is no less so. Note, (1.) The comforts we are most desirous of are sometimes found to bring along with them more occasion of trouble and uneasiness that we thought of; vanity being written upon all things under the sun, God thus teaches us to read it. (2.) We are too apt to be discontented with our comforts, because of the uneasiness that attends them. We know not when we are pleased; we know neither how to want nor how to abound. This struggle between Jacob and Esau in the womb represents the struggle that is maintained between the kingdom of God and the kingdom of Satan, [1.] In the world. The seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent have been contending ever since the enmity was put between them (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">ch. iii. 15</reference>), and this has occasioned a constant uneasiness among men. Christ himself came to <hi type="italic">send fire on earth, and this division,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.49">Luke xii. 49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.51">51</reference>. But let not this be offence to us. A holy war is better than the peace of the devil's palace. [2.] In the hearts of believers. No sooner is Christ formed in the soul than immediately there begins a conflict between the flesh and spirit, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.17">Gal. v. 17</reference>. The stream is not turned without a mighty struggle, which yet ought not to discourage us. It is better to have a conflict with sin than tamely to submit to it. <div eID="gen892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen893" type="x-p"/> 2. What course she took for her relief: <hi type="italic">She went to enquire of the Lord.</hi> Some think Melchizedek was now consulted as an oracle, or perhaps some <hi type="italic">Urim</hi> or <hi type="italic">Teraphim</hi> were now used to enquire of God by, as afterwards in the breast-plate of judgment. Note, The word and prayer, by both which we now enquire of the Lord, give great relief to those that are upon any account perplexed. It is a great relief to the mind to spread our case before the Lord, and ask counsel at his mouth. <hi type="italic">Go into the sanctuary,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen894" type="x-p"/> 3. The information given her, upon her enquiry, which expounded the mystery: <hi type="italic">Two nations are in thy womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.25.23">v. 23</reference>. She was now pregnant, not only with two children, but two nations, which should not only in their manners and dispositions greatly differ from each other, but in their interests clash and contend with each other; and the issue of the contest should be that the elder should serve the younger, which was fulfilled in the subjection of the Edomites, for many ages, to the house of David, till they revolted, <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.8">2 Chron. xxi. 8</reference>. Observe here, (1.) God is a free agent in dispensing his grace; it is his prerogative to make a difference between those who have not as yet themselves done either good or evil. This the apostle infers hence, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.12">Rom. ix. 12</reference>. (2.) In the struggle between grace and corruption in the soul, grace, the younger, shall certainly get the upper hand at last. <div eID="gen894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen895" type="x-p"/> III. That when they were born there was a great difference between them, which served to confirm what had been foretold (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.23">v. 23</reference>), was presage of the accomplishment of it, and served greatly to illustrate the type. <div eID="gen895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen896" type="x-p"/> 1. There was a great difference in their bodies, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.25">v. 25</reference>. Esau, when he was born, was rough and hairy, as if he had been already a grown man, whence he had his name <hi type="italic">Esau, made,</hi> reared already. This was an indication of a very strong constitution, and gave cause to expect that he would be a very robust, daring, active man. But Jacob was smooth and tender as other children. Note, (1.) The difference of men's capacities, and consequently of their condition in the world, arises very much from the difference of their natural constitution; some are plainly designed by nature for activity and honour, others as manifestly marked for obscurity. This instance of the divine sovereignty in the kingdom of providence may perhaps help to reconcile us to the doctrine of the divine sovereignty in the kingdom of grace. (2.) It is God's usual way to choose the weak things of the world, and to pass by the mighty, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26-1Cor.1.27">1 Cor. i. 26, 27</reference>. <div eID="gen896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen897" type="x-p"/> 2. There was a manifest contest in their births. Esau, the stronger, came forth first; but Jacob's hand <hi type="italic">took hold of his heel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.25.26">v. 26</reference>. This signified, (1.) Jacob's pursuit of the birthright and blessing; from the first, he reached forth to catch hold of it, and, if possible, to prevent his brother. (2.) His prevailing for it at last, that, in process of time, he should undermine his brother, and gain his point. This passage is referred to (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">Hos. xii. 8</reference>), and hence he had his name, <hi type="italic">Jacob, a supplanter.</hi> <div eID="gen897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen898" type="x-p"/> 3. They were very unlike in the temper of their minds, and the way of living they chose, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.27">v. 27</reference>. They soon appeared to be of very different dispositions. (1.) Esau was a man for this world. He was a man addicted to his sports, for he was a hunter; and a man who knew how to live by his wits, for he was a cunning hunter. Recreation was his business; he studied the art of it, and spent all his time in it. He never loved a book, nor cared for being within doors; but he was a man of the field, like Nimrod and Ishmael, all for the game, and never well but when he was upon the stretch in pursuit of it: in short, he set up for a gentleman and a soldier. (2.) Jacob was a man for the other world. He was not cut out for a statesman, nor did he affect to look great, but he was <hi type="italic">a plain man, dwelling in tents,</hi> an honest man that always meant well, and dealt fairly, that preferred the true delights of solitude and retirement to all the pretended pleasure of busy noisy sports: he dwelt in tents, [1.] As a shepherd. He was attached to that safe and silent employment of keeping sheep, to which also he bred up his children, <reference osisRef="Gen.46.34">ch. xlvi. 34</reference>. Or, [2.] As a student. He frequented the tents of Melchizedek, or Heber, as some understand it, to be taught by them divine things. And this was that son of Isaac on whom the covenant was entailed. <div eID="gen898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen899" type="x-p"/> 4. Their interest in the affections of their parents was likewise different. They had but these two children, and, it seems, one was the father's darling and the other the mother's, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.28">v. 28</reference>. (1.) Isaac, though he was not a stirring man himself (for when he went into the fields he went to meditate and pray, not to hunt), yet loved to have his son active. Esau knew how to please him, and showed a great respect for him, by treating him often with venison, which gained him the affections of the good old man, and won upon him more than one would have thought. (2.) Rebekah was mindful of the oracle of God, which had given the preference to Jacob, and therefore she preferred him in her love. And, if it be lawful for parents to make a difference between their children upon any account, doubtless Rebekah was in the right, that loved him whom God loved.
entries.18068a6726c37b294c11daa473d028308409e046: <div eID="gen899" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Esau Sells His Birthright. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1805.)</title> <div sID="gen900" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> And Jacob sod pottage: and Esau came from the field, and he <hi type="italic">was</hi> faint: <hi type="super">30</hi> And Esau said to Jacob, Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red <hi type="italic">pottage;</hi> for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> faint: therefore was his name called Edom. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Jacob said, Sell me this day thy birthright. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Esau said, Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> at the point to die: and what profit shall this birthright do to me? <hi type="super">33</hi> And Jacob said, Swear to me this day; and he sware unto him: and he sold his birthright unto Jacob. <hi type="super">34</hi> Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised <hi type="italic">his</hi> birthright. <div eID="gen900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen901" type="x-p"/> We have here a bargain made between Jacob and Esau about the birthright, which was Esau's by providence but Jacob's by promise. It was a spiritual privilege, including the excellency of dignity and the excellency of power, as well as the double portion, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.3">ch. xlix. 3</reference>. It seemed to be such a birthright as had then the blessing annexed to it, and the entail of the promise. Now see, <div eID="gen901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen902" type="x-p"/> I. Jacob's pious desire of the birthright, which yet he sought to obtain by indirect courses, not agreeable to his character as a plain man. It was not out of pride or ambition that he coveted the birthright, but with an eye to spiritual blessings, which he had got well acquainted with in his tents, while Esau had lost the scent of them in the field. For this he is to be commended, that he coveted earnestly the best gifts; yet in this he cannot be justified, that he took advantage of his brother's necessity to make him a very hard bargain (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sell me this day thy birthright.</hi> Probably there had formerly been some communication between them about this matter, and then it was not so great a surprise upon Esau as here it seems to be; and, it may be, Esau had sometimes spoken slightly of the birthright and its appurtenances, which encouraged Jacob to make this proposal to him. And, if so, Jacob is, in some measure, excusable in what he did to gain his point. Note, Plain men that have their conversation in simplicity and godly sincerity, and without worldly wisdom, are often found wisest of all for their souls and eternity. Those are wise indeed that are wise for another world. Jacob's wisdom appeared in two things:—1. He chose the fittest time, took the opportunity when it offered itself, and did not let it slip. 2. Having made the bargain, he made it sure, and got it confirmed by Esau's oath: <hi type="italic">Swear to me this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.25.33">v. 33</reference>. He took Esau when he was in the mind, and would not leave him a power of revocation. In a case of this nature, it is good to be sure. <div eID="gen902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen903" type="x-p"/> II. Esau's profane contempt of the birthright, and the foolish sale he made of it. He is called <hi type="italic">profane Esau</hi> for it (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">Heb. xii. 16</reference>), because <hi type="italic">for one morsel of meat he sold his birthright,</hi> as dear a morsel as ever was eaten since the forbidden fruit; and he lived to regret it when it was too late. Never was there such a foolish bargain as this which Esau now made; and yet he valued himself upon his policy, and had the reputation of a cunning man, and perhaps had often bantered his brother Jacob as a weak and simple man. Note, There are those that are penny-wise and pound-foolish, cunning hunters that can out-wit others and draw them into their snares, and yet are themselves imposed upon by Satan's wiles and led captive by him at his will. Again, God often chooses the foolish things of the world, by them to confound the wise. Plain Jacob makes a fool of cunning Esau. Observe the instances of Esau's folly. <div eID="gen903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen904" type="x-p"/> 1. His appetite was very strong, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.29-Gen.25.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. Poor Jacob had got some bread and pottage (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.29">v. 29</reference>) for his dinner, and was sitting down to it contentedly enough, without venison, when Esau came from hunting, hungry and weary, and perhaps had caught nothing. And now Jacob's pottage pleased his eye better than ever his game had done. Give me (says he) some of <hi type="italic">that red, that red,</hi> as it is in the original; it suited his own colour (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.25">v. 25</reference>), and, in reproach to him for this, he was ever afterwards called <hi type="italic">Edom, red.</hi> Nay, it should seem, he was so faint that he could not feed himself, nor had he a servant at hand to help him, but entreats his brother to feed him. Note, (1.) Those that addict themselves to sport <hi type="italic">weary themselves for very vanity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Hab. ii. 13</reference>. They might do the most needful business, and gain the greatest advantages, with half the pains they take, and half the perils they run into, in pursuit of their foolish pleasures. (2.) Those that work with quietness are more constantly and comfortably provided for than those that hunt with noise: bread is not always to the wise, but those that trust in the Lord and do good, verily they shall be fed, fed with daily bread; not as Esau, sometimes feasting and sometimes fainting. (3.) The gratifying of the sensual appetite is that which ruins thousands of precious souls: surely, if Esau was hungry and faint, he might have got a meal's meat cheaper than at the expense of his birthright; but he was unaccountably fond of the colour of this pottage, and could not deny himself the satisfaction of a mess of it, whatever it cost him. Never better can come of it, when men's <hi type="italic">hearts walk after their eyes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job xxxi. 7</reference>), and when they serve their own bellies: therefore look not thou upon the wine, or, as Esau, upon the pottage, when it is red, when it gives that colour in the cup, in the dish, which is most inviting, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.31">Prov. xxiii. 31</reference>. If we use ourselves to deny ourselves, we break the forces of most temptations. <div eID="gen904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen905" type="x-p"/> 2. His reasoning was very weak (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, I am at the point to die;</hi> and, if he were, would nothing serve to keep him alive but this pottage? If the famine were now in the land (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.1">ch. xxvi. 1</reference>), as Dr. Lightfoot conjectures, we cannot suppose Isaac so poor, or Rebekah so bad a house-keeper, but that he might have been supplied with food convenient, other ways, and might have saved his birthright: but his appetite has the mastery of him; he is in a longing condition, nothing will please him but this <hi type="italic">red</hi> this <hi type="italic">red pottage,</hi> and, to palliate his desire, he pretends he is at the point to die. If it had been so, was it not better for him to die in honour than to live in disgrace, to die under a blessing than to live under a curse? The birthright was typical of spiritual privileges, those of the church of the first-born. Esau was now tried how he would value them, and he shows himself sensible only of present grievances; may he but get relief against them, he cares not for his birthright. Better principled was Naboth, who would lose his life rather than sell his vineyard, because his part in the earthly Canaan signified his part in the heavenly, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.3">1 Kings xxi. 3</reference>. (1.) If we look on Esau's birthright as only a temporal advantage, what he said had something of truth in it, namely, that our worldly enjoyments, even those we are most fond of, will stand us in no stead in a dying hour (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.6-Ps.49.8">Ps. xlix. 6-8</reference>); they will not put by the stroke of death, nor ease the pangs nor remove the sting: yet Esau, who set up for a gentleman, should have had a greater and more noble spirit than to sell even such an honour so cheaply. (2.) But, being of a spiritual nature, his undervaluing it was the greatest profaneness imaginable. Note, It is egregious folly to part with our interest in God, and Christ, and heaven, for the riches, honours, and pleasures, of this world, as bad a bargain as his that sold a birthright for a dish of broth. <div eID="gen905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen906" type="x-p"/> 3. Repentance was hidden from his eyes (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">He did eat and drink,</hi> pleased his palate, satisfied his cravings, congratulated himself on the good meal's meat he had had, and then carelessly rose up and went his way, without any serious reflections upon the bad bargain he had made, or any show of regret. Thus Esau despised his birthright; he used no means at all to get the bargain revoked, made no appeal to his father about it, nor proposed to his brother to compound the matter; but the bargain which his necessity had made (supposing it were so) his profaneness confirmed <hi type="italic">ex post facto—after the deed;</hi> and by his subsequent neglect and contempt he did, as it were, acknowledge a fine, and by justifying himself in what he had done he put the bargain past recall. Note, People are ruined, not so much by doing what is amiss, as by doing it and not repenting of it, doing it and standing to it.  <chapter eID="Gen.25"/> <div eID="gen906" type="x-p"/>

entries.8dd865bca5fe55a9f18744c278b6b87b248d3c8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv270"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.25.1-Gen.25.6">Ge 25:1-6</reference>. Sons of Abraham.</title> <div sID="gen448" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv270"/><hi type="bold">1. Abraham took a wife--</hi>rather, "had taken"; for Keturah is called Abraham's concubine, or secondary wife (<reference osisRef="1Chr.1.32">1Ch 1:32</reference>); and as, from her bearing six sons to him, it is improbable that he married after Sarah's death; and also as he sent them all out to seek their own independence, during his lifetime, it is clear that this marriage is related here out of its chronological order, merely to form a proper winding up of the patriarch's history. <div eID="gen448" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fd68931eba5dfe82a132496e058af9307246948: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv271"/><div sID="gen449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv271"/><hi type="bold">5-6. Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac ... unto the sons of the concubines ... Abraham gave gifts--</hi>While the chief part of the inheritance went to Isaac; the other sons (Ishmael included) migrated to "the East country," that is, Arabia, but received each a portion of the patrimony, perhaps in cattle and other things; and this settlement of Abraham's must have given satisfaction, since it is still the rule followed among the pastoral tribes. <div eID="gen449" type="x-p"/>
entries.80bc1364b8b7f56f18bb500949d8fa2933a15ded: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv272"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.25.7-Gen.25.11">Ge 25:7-11</reference>. Death of Abraham.</title> <div sID="gen450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv272"/><hi type="bold">7. these are the days of ... Abraham--</hi>His death is here related, though he lived till Jacob and Esau were fifteen years, just one hundred years after coming to Canaan; "the father of the faithful," "the friend of God" [Jas 2:23], died; and even in his death, the promises were fulfilled (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.15.15">Ge 15:15</reference>). We might have wished some memorials of his deathbed experience; but the Spirit of God has withheld them--nor was it necessary; for (see <reference osisRef="Matt.7.16">Mt 7:16</reference>) from earth he passed into heaven (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.22">Lu 16:22</reference>). Though dead he yet liveth (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.32">Mt 22:32</reference>). <div eID="gen450" type="x-p"/>
entries.09d3f0195c972572c4aa74e6e3ceccbc239a6d5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv273"/><div sID="gen451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv273"/><hi type="bold">9-10. his sons ... buried him--</hi>Death often puts an end to strife, reconciles those who have been alienated, and brings rival relations, as in this instance, to mingle tears over a father's grave. <div eID="gen451" type="x-p"/>
entries.bad79e4a76b2a9f85abbff8d5f0c62d52b54fc2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv274"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.25.12-Gen.25.18">Ge 25:12-18</reference>. Descendants of Ishmael. Before passing to the line of the promised seed, the historian gives a brief notice of Ishmael, to show that the promises respecting that son of Abraham were fulfilled--first, in the greatness of his posterity (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.17.20">Ge 17:20</reference>); and, secondly, in their independence.</title> <div sID="gen452" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv274"/><hi type="bold">18. he died--</hi>rather, "it [their lot] fell" in the presence of his brethren (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Ge 16:12</reference>). <div eID="gen452" type="x-p"/>
entries.f605fc81f342ea0a61756a88f3d6ff025c8d30c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv275"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.25.19-Gen.25.34">Ge 25:19-34</reference>. History of Isaac.</title> <div sID="gen453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv275"/><hi type="bold">19. these are the generations--</hi>account of the leading events in his life. <div eID="gen453" type="x-p"/>
entries.75f58c4d9a289e15d798cf8c80968d0ccaf0a65d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv276"/><div sID="gen454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv276"/><hi type="bold">21. Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife--</hi>Though tried in a similar way to his father, he did not follow the same crooked policy. Twenty years he continued unblessed with offspring, whose seed was to be "as the stars" [Ge 26:4]. But in answer to their mutual prayers (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1Pe 3:7</reference>), Rebekah was divinely informed that she was to be the mother of twins, who should be the progenitors of two independent nations; that the descendants of the younger should be the more powerful and subdue those of the other (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.12">Ro 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.8">2Ch 21:8</reference>). <div eID="gen454" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c65cabfa36e71a76e2c9070429812867d3da977: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv277"/><div sID="gen455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv277"/><hi type="bold">27. the boys grew--</hi>from the first, opposite to each other in character, manners, and habits. <div eID="gen455" type="x-p"/>
entries.027de82db14cb919f11975063a67a6f6004fb47c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv278"/><div sID="gen456" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv278"/>28. The parents were divided in their affection; and while the grounds, at least of the father's partiality, were weak, the distinction made between the children led, as such conduct always does, to unhappy consequences. <div eID="gen456" type="x-p"/>
entries.b21d41b772b9024d1360be8ac45fa1b743f135c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv279"/><div sID="gen457" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv279"/><hi type="bold">29. Jacob sod pottage--</hi>made of lentils or small beans, which are common in Egypt and Syria. It is probable that it was made of Egyptian beans, which Jacob had procured as a dainty; for Esau was a stranger to it. It is very palatable; and to the weary hunter, faint with hunger, its odor must have been irresistibly tempting. <div eID="gen457" type="x-p"/>
entries.297f30a1fb3a84096ad756dd71ba43d846ca858f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv280"/><div sID="gen458" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv280"/><hi type="bold">31. Jacob said, Sell me ... thy birthright--</hi>that is, the rights and privileges of the first-born, which were very important, the chief being that they were the family priests (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Ex 4:22</reference>) and had a double portion of the inheritance (<reference osisRef="Deut.21.17">De 21:17</reference>). <div eID="gen458" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e2c30b0dae21e95390ca14ee207003816cb857f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv281"/><div sID="gen459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv281"/><hi type="bold">32. Esau said ... I am at the point to die--</hi>that is, I am running daily risk of my life; and of what use will the birthright be to me: so he despised or cared little about it, in comparison with gratifying his appetite--he threw away his religious privileges for a trifle; and thence he is styled "a profane person" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job 31:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.6.13">6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>). "There was never any meat, except the forbidden fruit, so dear bought, as this broth of Jacob" [Bishop Hall]. <chapter eID="Gen.25"/>

entries.e22f78d5950d5790da96912a2b9384905b04de58: <div eID="gen1132" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen1133" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1134" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1134" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1133" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1135" type="x-p"/> Abraham marries Keturah, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.1">Gen 25:1</reference>. Their issue, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.2-Gen.25.4">Gen 25:2-4</reference>. Makes Isaac his heir, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.5">Gen 25:5</reference>; but gives portions to the sons of his concubines, and sends them eastward from Isaac, to find settlements, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.6">Gen 25:6</reference>. Abraham's age, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.7">Gen 25:7</reference>, and death, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.8">Gen 25:8</reference>. Is buried by his sons Isaac and Ishmael in the cave of Machpelah, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.9">Gen 25:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.10">Gen 25:10</reference>. God's blessing upon Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.11">Gen 25:11</reference>. The generations of Ishmael, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.12-Gen.25.16">Gen 25:12-16</reference>. His age, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.17">Gen 25:17</reference>, and death, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.18">Gen 25:18</reference>. Of the generations of Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.19">Gen 25:19</reference>, who was married in his fortieth year, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.20">Gen 25:20</reference>. Rebekah his wife being barren, on his prayer to God she conceives, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.21">Gen 25:21</reference>. She inquires of the Lord concerning her state, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.22">Gen 25:22</reference>. The Lord's answer, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.23">Gen 25:23</reference>. She is delivered of twins, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.24">Gen 25:24</reference>. Peculiarities in the birth of her sons Esau and Jacob, from which they had their names, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.25">Gen 25:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.26">Gen 25:26</reference>. Their different manner of life, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.27">Gen 25:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.28">Gen 25:28</reference>. Esau, returning from the field faint, begs pottage from his brother, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.29">Gen 25:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.30">Gen 25:30</reference>. Jacob refuses to grant him any but on condition of his selling him his birthright, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.31">Gen 25:31</reference>. Esau, ready to die, parts with his birthright to save his life, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.32">Gen 25:32</reference>. Jacob causes him to confirm the sale with an oath, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.33">Gen 25:33</reference>. He receives bread and pottage of lentils, and departs, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.34">Gen 25:34</reference>. <div eID="gen1135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1136" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen1136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1137" type="x-p"/> Then again Abraham took a wife - When Abraham took Keturah we are not informed; it might have been in the lifetime of Sarah; and the original ויסף vaiyoseph, and he added, etc., seems to give some countenance to this opinion. Indeed it is not very likely that he had the children mentioned here after the death of Sarah; and from the circumstances of his age, feebleness, etc., at the birth of Isaac, it is still more improbable. Even at that age, forty years before the marriage of Isaac, the birth of his son is considered as not less miraculous on his part than on the part of Sarah; for the apostle expressly says, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.19">Rom 4:19</reference>, that Abraham considered not his own body Now Dead, when he was about a hundred years old, nor the Deadness of Sarah's womb; hence we learn that they were both past the procreation of children, insomuch that the birth of Isaac is ever represented as supernatural. It is therefore very improbable that he had any child after the birth of Isaac; and therefore we may well suppose that Moses had related this transaction out of its chronological order, which is not infrequent in the sacred writings, when a variety of important facts relative to the accomplishment of some grand design are thought necessary to be produced in a connected series. On this account intervening matters of a different complexion are referred to a future time. Perhaps we may be justified in reading the verse: "And Abraham had added, and had taken a wife (besides Hagar) whose name was Keturah," etc. The chronology in the margin dates this marriage with Keturah A. M. 2154, nine years after the death of Sarah, A. M. 2145. Jonathan ben Uzziel and the Jerusalem Targum both assert that Keturah was the same as Hagar. Some rabbins, and with them Dr. Hammond, are of the same opinion; but both Hagar and Keturah are so distinguished in the Scriptures, that the opinion seems destitute of probability.
entries.5a87c79f2aac2a31dcfa491dd8bc70faf6aa8e03: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen1137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1138" type="x-p"/> Zimran - Stephanus Byzantinus mentions a city in Arabia Felix called Zadram, which some suppose to have been named from this son of Keturah; but it is more likely, as Calmet observes, that all these sons of Abraham resided in Arabia Deserta; and Pliny, Hist. Nat., lib. vi., c. 28, mentions a people in that country called Zamarenians, who were probably the descendants of this person. <div eID="gen1138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1139" type="x-p"/> Jokshan - Several learned men have been of opinion that this Jokshan was the same as Kachtan, the father of the Arabs. The testimonies in favor of this opinion see in Dr. Hunt's Oration, De Antiquitate, etc., Linguae Arabicae, p. 4. Calmet supposes that the Cataneans, who inhabited a part of Arabia Deserta, sprang from this Jokshan. <div eID="gen1139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1140" type="x-p"/> Medan, and Midian - Probably those who peopled that part of Arabia Petraea contiguous to the land of Moab eastward of the Dead Sea. St. Jerome terms the people of this country Madinaeans; and Ptolemy mentions a people called Madianites, who dwelt in the same place. <div eID="gen1140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1141" type="x-p"/> Ishbak - From this person Calmet supposes the brook Jabbok, which has its source in the mountains of Gilead, and falls into the sea of Tiberias, took its name. <div eID="gen1141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1142" type="x-p"/> Shuah - Or Shuach. From this man the Sacceans, near to Batanla, at the extremity of Arabia Deserta, towards Syria, are supposed to have sprung. Bildad the Shuhite, one of Job's friends, is supposed to have descended from this son of Abraham.
entries.a91faf3b77772af2dad8ae42c2d5a9a4b8441332: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen1142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1143" type="x-p"/> Sheba - From whom sprang the Sabeans, who robbed Job of his cattle. See Bochart and Calmet. <div eID="gen1143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1144" type="x-p"/> Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim - We know not who these were, but as each name is plural they must have been tribes or families, and not individuals. Onkelos interprets these words of persons dwelling in camps, tents, and islands; and Jonathan ben Uzziel calls them merchants, artificers, and heads or chiefs of people.
entries.c039250865e724217dd704d15dd52baa90dedf80: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen1144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1145" type="x-p"/> Ephah, and Epher, etc. - Of these we know no more than of the preceding; an abundance of conjectures is already furnished by the commentators.
entries.ca4e92256489ad55db027c17d61580f6bb28c848: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen1145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1146" type="x-p"/> Gave all that he had unto Isaac - His principal flocks, and especially his right to the land of Canaan, including a confirmation to him and his posterity of whatever was contained in the promises of God.
entries.3719fcf11b451ad8460ece41ec7b82035b424f2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen1146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1147" type="x-p"/> Unto the sons of the concubines - Viz., Hagar and Keturah, Abraham gave gifts. Cattle for breed, seed to sow the land, and implements for husbandry, may be what is here intended. <div eID="gen1147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1148" type="x-p"/> And sent them away - while he yet lived - Lest after his death they should dispute a settlement in the Land of Promise with Isaac; therefore he very prudently sent them to procure settlements during his lifetime, that they might be under no temptation to dispute the settlement with Isaac in Canaan. From this circumstance arose that law which has prevailed in almost all countries, of giving the estates to the eldest son by a lawful wife; for though concubines, or wives of the second rank, were perfectly legitimate in those ancient times, yet their children did not inherit, except in case of the failure of legal issue, and with the consent of the lawful wife; and it is very properly observed by Calmet, that it was in consequence of the consent of Leah and Rachel that the children of their slaves by Jacob had a common and equal lot with the rest. By a law of Solon all natural children were excluded from the paternal inheritance, but their fathers were permitted to give them any sum not beyond a thousand drachma by way of present. Eastward, unto the east country - Arabia Deserta, which was eastward of Beer-sheba, where Abraham lived.
entries.396e58622d4f87a8337ffbc550e0df86dbc6836c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen1148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1149" type="x-p"/> The days of the years, etc. - There is a beauty in this expression which is not sufficiently regarded. Good men do not live by centuries, though many such have lived several hundred years, nor do they count their lives even by years, but by days, living as if they were the creatures only of A Day; having no more time than they can with any propriety call their own, and living that day in reference to eternity.
entries.5660229a40edf8ca47df684eebd7073f1b6ed62e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen1149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1150" type="x-p"/> Then Abraham gave up the ghost - Highly as I value our translation for general accuracy, fidelity, and elegance, I must beg leave to dissent from this version. The original word יגוע yigva, from the root גוע gava, signifies to pant for breath, to expire, to cease from breathing, or to breathe one's last; and here, and wherever the original word is used, the simple term expired would be the proper expression. In our translation this expression occurs <reference osisRef="Gen.25.8">Gen 25:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.17">Gen 25:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">Gen 35:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.44.33">Gen 44:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.3.11">Job 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.18">Job 10:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.20">Job 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.19">Job 13:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.10">Job 14:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.19">Lam 1:19</reference>; in all of which places the original is גוע gava. It occurs also in our translation, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.9">Jer 15:9</reference>, but there the original is נפחה נפשה naphecah naphshah, she breathed out her soul; the verb גוע gava not being used. Now as our English word ghost, from the Anglo-Saxon gast, an inmate, inhabitant, guest, (a casual visitant), also a spirit, is now restricted among us to the latter meaning, always signifying the immortal spirit or soul of man, the guest of the body; and as giving up the spirit, ghost, or soul, is an act not proper to man, though commending it to God, in our last moments, is both an act of faith and piety; and as giving up the ghost, i.e., dismissing his spirit from his body, is attributed to Jesus Christ, to whom alone it is proper, I therefore object against its use in every other case. <div eID="gen1150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1151" type="x-p"/> Every man since the fall has not only been liable to death, but has deserved it, as all have forfeited their lives because of sin. Jesus Christ, as born immaculate, and having never sinned, had not forfeited his life, and therefore may be considered as naturally and properly immortal. No man, says he, taketh it - my life, from me, but I lay it down of myself; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again: therefore doth the Father love me, because I lay down my life that I might take it again, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.17">Joh 10:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.18">Joh 10:18</reference>. Hence we rightly translate <reference osisRef="Mat.27.50">Mat 27:50</reference>, αφηκε το πνευμα, he gave up the ghost; i.e., he dismissed his spirit that he might die for the sin of the world. The Evangelist St. <reference osisRef="Joh.19.30">Joh 19:30</reference>, makes use of an expression to the same import, which we translate in the same way, παρεδωκε το πνευμα, he delivered up his spirit. We translate <reference osisRef="Mar.15.37">Mar 15:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Luk.23.46">Luk 23:46</reference>, he gave up the ghost, but not correctly, because the word in both these places is very different, εξεπνευσε, he breathed his last, or expired, though in the latter place (<reference osisRef="Luk.23.46">Luk 23:46</reference>) there is an equivalent expression, O Father, into thy hands παρατιθεμαι το πνευμα μου, I commit my spirit, i.e., I place my soul in thy hand; proving that the act was his own, that no man could take his life away from him, that he did not die by the perfidy of his disciple, or the malice of the Jews, but by his own free act. Thus He Laid Down his life for the sheep. Of Ananias and Sapphira, <reference osisRef="Act.5.5">Act 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.5.10">Act 5:10</reference>, and of Herod, <reference osisRef="Act.12.23">Act 12:23</reference>, our translation says they gave up the ghost; but the word in both places is εξεψυξε, which simply means to breathe out, to expire, or die; but in no case, either by the Septuagint in the Old or any of the sacred writers in the New Testament, is αφηκε το μνευμα or παρεδωκε το πνευμα, he dismissed his spirit or delivered up his spirit, spoken of any person but Christ. Abraham, Isaac, Ishmael, Jacob, etc., breathed their last; Ananias, Sapphira, and Herod expired; but none, Jesus Christ excepted, gave up the ghost, dismissed, or delivered up his own spirit, and was consequently free among the dead. Of the patriarchs, etc., the Septuagint uses the word εκλειπων, failing, or κατεπαυσε, he ceased or rested. <div eID="gen1151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1152" type="x-p"/> An old man - Viz., one hundred and seventy-five, the youngest of all the patriarchs; and full of years. The word years is not in the text; but as our translators saw that some word was necessary to fill up the text, they added this in italics. It is probable that the true word is ימים yamim, days, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">Gen 35:29</reference>; and this reading is found in several of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., in the Samaritan text, Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, Persic, and Chaldee. On these authorities it might be safely admitted into the text. <div eID="gen1152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1153" type="x-p"/> Being full of days, or full of years - To be satiated with days or life, has been in use among different nations to express the termination of life, and especially life ended without reluctance. It seems to be a metaphor taken from a guest regaled by a plentiful banquet, and is thus used by the Roman poets. Lucretius, lib. iii., ver. 947, ridiculing those who were unreasonably attached to life, and grievously afflicted at the prospect of death, addresses them in the following manner: - <div eID="gen1153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1154" type="x-p"/> Quid mortem congemis, ac fies? <div eID="gen1154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1155" type="x-p"/> Nam si grata fuit tibi vita anteacta, priorque, <div eID="gen1155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1156" type="x-p"/> Et non omnia pertusum congesta quasi in vas <div eID="gen1156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1157" type="x-p"/> Commoda perfluxere, atque ingrata interiere: <div eID="gen1157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1158" type="x-p"/> Cur non, ut Plenus Vitae Conviva, Recedis? <div eID="gen1158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1159" type="x-p"/> Fond mortal, what's the matter, thou dost sigh? <div eID="gen1159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1160" type="x-p"/> Why all these fears because thou once must die? <div eID="gen1160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1161" type="x-p"/> For if the race thou hast already run <div eID="gen1161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1162" type="x-p"/> Was pleasant, if with joy thou saw'st the sun, <div eID="gen1162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1163" type="x-p"/> If all thy pleasures did not pass thy mind <div eID="gen1163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1164" type="x-p"/> As through a sieve, but left some sweets behind, <div eID="gen1164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1165" type="x-p"/> Why dost thou not then, like a Thankful Guest, <div eID="gen1165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1166" type="x-p"/> Rise cheerfully from life's Abundant Feast? <div eID="gen1166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1167" type="x-p"/> Creech. <div eID="gen1167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1168" type="x-p"/> Et nec opinanti mors ad caput astitit ante, <div eID="gen1168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1169" type="x-p"/> Quam Satur, ac Plenus possis discedere rerum <div eID="gen1169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1170" type="x-p"/> Ib. ver. 972. <div eID="gen1170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1171" type="x-p"/> And unexpected hasty death destroys, <div eID="gen1171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1172" type="x-p"/> Before thy greedy mind is Full of Joys. Idem. <div eID="gen1172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1173" type="x-p"/> Horace makes use of the same figure: - <div eID="gen1173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1174" type="x-p"/> Inde fit, ut raro, qui se vixisse beatum <div eID="gen1174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1175" type="x-p"/> Dicat, et exacto Contentus tempore vitae <div eID="gen1175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1176" type="x-p"/> Cedat, ut Conviva Satur, reperire queamus. <div eID="gen1176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1177" type="x-p"/> Sat. l. i. Sat. i. ver. 117. <div eID="gen1177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1178" type="x-p"/> From hence how few, like Sated Guests, depart From life's Full Banquet with a cheerful heart? <div eID="gen1178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1179" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen1179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1180" type="x-p"/> The same image is expressed with strong ridicule in his last Epistle - <div eID="gen1180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1181" type="x-p"/> Lusisti satis, edisti satis, atque bibisti; <div eID="gen1181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1182" type="x-p"/> Tempus Abire tibi est. <div eID="gen1182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1183" type="x-p"/> Epist. l. ii., ver. 216. <div eID="gen1183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1184" type="x-p"/> Thou hast eaten, drunk, and play'd Enough; then why So stark reluctant to leave off, and Die? <div eID="gen1184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1185" type="x-p"/> The poet Statius uses abire paratum Plenum vita, "prepared to depart, being Full of Life," in exactly the same sense: - <div eID="gen1185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1186" type="x-p"/> Dubio quem non in turbine rerum <div eID="gen1186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1187" type="x-p"/> Deprendet suprema dies; sed abire paratum, <div eID="gen1187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1188" type="x-p"/> Acts Plenum Vita. Sylv. l. ii., Villa Surrentina, ver. 128. <div eID="gen1188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1189" type="x-p"/> The man whose mighty soul is not immersed in dubious whirl of secular concerns, His final hour ne'er takes him by surprise, But, Full of Life, he stands Prepared to Die. <div eID="gen1189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1190" type="x-p"/> It was the opinion of Aristotle that a man should depart from life as he should rise from a banquet. Thus Abraham died Full of days, and Satisfied with life, but in a widely different spirit from that recommended by the above writers - He left life with a hope full of immortality, which they could never boast; for He saw the day of Christ, and was glad; and his hope was crowned, for here it is expressly said, He was gathered to his fathers; surely not to the bodies of his sleeping ancestors, who were buried in Chaldea and not in Canaan, nor with his fathers in any sense, for he was deposited in the cave where his Wife alone slept; but he was gathered to the spirits of just men made perfect, and to the Church of the first-born, whose names are written in heaven; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">Heb 12:23</reference>.
entries.bb6d62796305ef52a6019c720a863da3bcc3be73: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen1190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1191" type="x-p"/> His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him - Though Ishmael and his mother had been expelled from Abraham's family on the account of Isaac, yet, as he was under the same obligation to a most loving affectionate father as his brother Isaac, if any personal feuds remained, they agreed to bury them on this occasion, that both might dutifully join in doing the last offices to a parent who was an honor to them and to human nature: and, considering the rejection of Ishmael from the inheritance, this transaction shows his character in an amiable point of view; for though he was a wild man, (see <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen 16:12</reference>), yet this appellation appears to be more characteristic of his habits of life than of his disposition. <div eID="gen1191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1192" type="x-p"/> For the character of Abraham see the conclusion of this chapter, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.34">Gen 25:34</reference> (note).
entries.35113af3f8d985c260c512210f7941a2f4dc2914: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen1192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1193" type="x-p"/> God blessed his son Isaac - The peculiar blessings and influences by which Abraham had been distinguished now rested upon Isaac; but how little do we hear in him of the work of faith, the patience of hope, and the labor of love! Only one Abraham and one Christ ever appeared among men; there have been some successful imitators, there should have been many.
entries.3e556fccef0e791836741f68d6ee2d39106b9b0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen1193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1194" type="x-p"/> These are the generations of Ishmael - The object of the inspired writer seems to be to show how the promises of God were fulfilled to both the branches of Abraham's family. Isaac has been already referred to; God blessed him according to the promise. He had also promised to multiply Ishmael, and an account of his generation is introduced to show how exactly the promise had also been fulfilled to him.
entries.93ff25aea6f5fd210f02716630a3937afdc5abfd: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen1194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1195" type="x-p"/> Nebajoth - From whom came the Nabatheans, whose capital was Petra, or, according to Strabo, Nabathea. They dwelt in Arabia Petraea, and extended themselves on the east towards Arabia Deserta. <div eID="gen1195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1196" type="x-p"/> Kedar - The founder of the Cedreans, who dwelt near to the Nabatheans. The descendants of Kedar form a part of the Saracens. <div eID="gen1196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1197" type="x-p"/> Adbeel, and Mibsam - Where these were situated is not known.
entries.491d3e78086dedc10b3b5b9755c3888597489652: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen1197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1198" type="x-p"/> Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa - Where the first and last of these settled is not known; but it is probable that Dumah gave his name to a place called Dumah in Arabia. See a prophecy concerning this place, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Isa 21:11</reference> (note), from which we find that it was in the vicinity of Mount Seir. <div eID="gen1198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1199" type="x-p"/> These three names have passed into a proverb among the Hebrews, because of their signification. משמע mishma signifies Hearing; דומה dumah, Silence; and משא massa, Patience. Hence, "Hear much, say little, and bear much," tantamount to the famous maxim of the Stoics, Ανεχου και απεχου, "Sustain and abstain," is supposed to be the spirit of the original words.
entries.40ab5725b24f6c9bdf35f37bc289100a3bf558e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen1199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1200" type="x-p"/> Hadar - This name should be read Hadad as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.30">1Chr 1:30</reference>. This reading is supported by more than three hundred MSS., versions, and printed editions. See Clarke at <reference osisRef="Gen.25.18">Gen 25:18</reference> (note). <div eID="gen1200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1201" type="x-p"/> Tema - Supposed to be a place in Arabia Deserta, the same of which Job speaks, <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference>. <div eID="gen1201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1202" type="x-p"/> Jetur - From whom came the Itureans, who occupied a small tract of country beyond Jordan, which was afterwards possessed by the half-tribe of Manasseh. <div eID="gen1202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1203" type="x-p"/> Naphish - These are evidently the same people mentioned <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.19">1Chr 5:19</reference>, who, with the Itureans and the people of Nadab, assisted the Hagarenes against the Israelites, but were overcome by the two tribes of Reuben and Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. <div eID="gen1203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1204" type="x-p"/> Kedemah - Probably the descendants of this person dwelt at Kedemoth, a place mentioned <reference osisRef="Deu.2.26">Deu 2:26</reference>. I wish the reader to observe, that concerning those ancient tribes mentioned here or elsewhere in the Pentateuch little is known; nor of their places of settlement have we more certain information. On this subject many learned men have toiled hard with but little fruit of their labor. Those who wish to enter into discussions of this nature must consult Bochart's Geographia Sacra, Calmet, etc.
entries.bcdcad1096de207b2ae7fa1d3fc4d215c1880749: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen1204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1205" type="x-p"/> These are their names - By which their descendants were called. Their towns - places of encampment in the wilderness, such as have been used by the Arabs from the remotest times. Their castles, טירתם tirotham, their towers, probably mountain tops, fortified rocks, and fastnesses of various kinds in woods and hilly countries.
entries.841fbc1643fd521e3d2b8ce2f55dde4628653c18: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen1205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1206" type="x-p"/> They dwelt from Havilah unto Shur - The descendants of Ishmael possessed all that country which extends from east to west, from Havilah on the Euphrates, near its junction with the Tigris, to the desert of Shur eastward of Egypt; and which extends along the isthmus of Suez, which separates the Red Sea from the Mediterranean. <div eID="gen1206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1207" type="x-p"/> As thou goest toward Assyria - "These words," says Calmet, "may refer either to Egypt, to Shur, or to Havilah. The desert of Shur is on the road from Egypt to Assyria in traversing Arabia Petraea, and in passing by the country of Havilah. I know not," adds he, "whether Ashshurah in the text may not mark out rather the Asshurim descended from Keturah, than the Assyrians, who were the descendants of Asshur the son of Shem." <div eID="gen1207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1208" type="x-p"/> He died in the presence of all his brethren - The original will not well bear this translation. In <reference osisRef="Gen.25.17">Gen 25:17</reference> it is said, He gave up the ghost and died, and was gathered to his people. Then follows the account of the district occupied by the Ishmaelites, at the conclusion of which it is added על פני כל אחיו נפל al peney col echaiv naphal, "It (the lot or district) Fell (or was divided to him) in the presence of all his brethren:" and this was exactly agreeable to the promise of God, <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen 16:12</reference>, He shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren; and to show that this promise had been strictly fulfilled, it is here remarked that his lot or inheritance was assigned him by Divine Providence, contiguous to that of the other branches of the family. The same word, נפל naphal, is used <reference osisRef="Jos.23.4">Jos 23:4</reference>, for to divide by lot. <div eID="gen1208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1209" type="x-p"/> On the subject of writing the same proper name variously in our common Bibles, the following observations and tables will not be unacceptable to the reader. "Men who have read their Bible with care," says Dr. Kennicott, "must have remarked that the name of the same person is often expressed differently in different places. Indeed the variation is sometimes so great that we can scarcely persuade ourselves that one and the same person is really meant. A uniform expression of proper names is diligently attended to in other books: perhaps in every other book, except the Old Testament. But here we find strange variety in the expression, and consequently great confusion: and indeed there is scarcely any one general source of error which calls for more careful correction than the same proper names now wrongly expressed. I shall add here, from the Pentateuch, some proper names which are strangely varied: first, twenty-three names expressed differently in the Hebrew text itself, and seventeen of them in our English translation; and then thirty-one names expressed uniformly in the Hebrew yet differently in the English. "Nothing can be more clear than that these fifty-four proper names (at least the far greater part of them) should be expressed with the very same letters, in the places where they are now different. In the second list, instances 6, 10, and 13, have been corrected and expressed uniformly in the English Bible printed at Oxford in 1769. And surely the same justice in the translation should be done to the rest of these proper names, and to all others through the Bible; at least, where the original words are now properly the same. Who would not wonder at seeing the same persons named both Simon and Shimon, Richard and Ricard? And can we then admit here both Seth and Sheth, Rachel and Rahel? Again: whoever could admit (as above) both Gaza and Azzak, with Rameses and Raamses, should not object to London and Ondon, with Amsterdam and Amstradam. In short, in a history far more interesting than any other, the names of persons and places should be distinguished accurately, and defined with exact uniformity. And no true critic will think lightly of this advice of Origen, Contemnenda non est accurata circa Nomina diligentia ei, qui volurit probe intelligere sanctas literas? No person who desires thoroughly to understand the sacred writings, should undervalue a scrupulous attention to the proper names." - Kennicott's Remarks.
entries.e7134c598bd6525d7f426702d05b4f270755bd66: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen1209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1210" type="x-p"/> These are the generations of Isaac - This is the history of Isaac and his family. Here the sixth section of the law begins, called תולדת יעחק toledoth yitschak; as the fifth, called חיי שרה chaiye Sarah, which begins with Genesis 23, ends at the preceding verse.
entries.8f0c0b00dd72a06890b0372e97952753f09dfd9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen1210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1211" type="x-p"/> Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife - Isaac and Rebekah had now lived nineteen years together without having a child; for he was forty years old when he married Rebekah, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.20">Gen 25:20</reference>, and he was threescore years of age when Jacob and Esau were born, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.26">Gen 25:26</reference>. Hence it is evident they had lived nineteen years together without having a child. <div eID="gen1211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1212" type="x-p"/> The form of the original in this place is worthy of notice: Isaac entreated Jehovah, לנכח אשתו lenochach ishto, directly, purposely, especially, for his wife. Ainsworth thinks the words imply their praying together for this thing; and the rabbins say that "Isaac and Rebekah went on purpose to Mount Moriah, where he had been bound, and prayed together there that they might have a son." God was pleased to exercise the faith of Isaac previous to the birth of Jacob, as he had exercised that of Abraham previous to his own birth.
entries.cc8b29d31944937a509d191cce788563ee1b3081: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen1212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1213" type="x-p"/> The children struggled together - יתרצצו yithrotsatsu, they dashed against or bruised each other, there was a violent agitation, so that the mother was apprehensive both of her own and her children's safety; and, supposing this was an uncommon case, she went to inquire of the Lord, as the good women in the present day would go to consult a surgeon or physician; for intercourse with God is not so common now, as it was in those times of great primitive simplicity.
